summary: A 1974 note proposing standard file formats for sending documents across different computer environments. The aim was to let a document sent from one kind of system be read on another. Its status is unknown.

plainLanguage.summary: Different computers write files in different ways. This note suggests a shared way so everyone can read the same file.

subtitle: Standard file formats for document interchange across different systems

tldr.problem: Different computer systems use different file formats, making it difficult to exchange documents across systems and networks.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines six standard document formats, each with a specified character set (ASCII), page dimensions (in lines and characters), and format control procedures (form feeds, line feeds, tabs), allowing authors to advertise files in a standard format.
tldr.outcome: Documents prepared in a standard format can be transferred and printed on different systems with predictable results.

today: RFC 678 proposed document format standards in 1974. These specific formats are obsolete, superseded by modern document standards like PDF and Unicode-based formats, but the principle of standardized format definitions remains important for document interchange.

sections.title: The Problem of Document Portability
sections.content:
RFC 678 addresses the problem of sharing online documents across the diverse computers and networks of the 1970s. When one system prepares a document file and another system tries to print or display it, differences in how the two systems handle files—character sets, line lengths, page breaks, spacing—create readability and printing problems.

The RFC proposes that instead of trying to convert files between many different local formats, the network community should adopt a set of standard formats. An author who prepares a document in one of these standard formats can advertise the format name, and users can retrieve and print the file with confidence in how it will appear.
sections.plainLanguage: Different kinds of computers write and print files in different ways, which makes sharing documents hard. This note suggests standard ways of writing that everyone can handle.

sections.title: The Six Standard Formats
sections.content:
The RFC defines six formats, each suited to different printing environments. Format 1 (Basic Document) uses 60-line pages, 72 characters wide, with form feeds and line feeds, for line printers that enforce 3-line margins. Format 2 (Terminal) supports 66-line pages and hard-copy terminals with backspace and other format controls. Format 3 (Line Printer) fits full-width 132-character line printer paper. Format 4 (Card Image) simulates punched-card input with 80 characters per card. Format 5 (Center Document) formats 60 lines for printers with margins, centered on the page. Format 6 (Bound Document) similarly formats 60 lines but with asymmetric margins to leave room for binding.

All formats use the Network Virtual Terminal (NVT) ASCII code character set with the high order bit zero, ensuring compatibility across systems.
sections.plainLanguage: The six formats describe different page sizes and margins for different kinds of printers: line printers, terminals, card readers, and devices with margins for binding.

sections.title: Format Controls and Page Geometry
sections.content:
Each format specifies its active format effectors—the ASCII control codes that the printer will obey. These include Form Feed (moves to the next logical page), Carriage Return (moves to the left edge), Line Feed (moves to the next line), Horizontal Tab (moves to the next tab stop), and Back Space (moves one character left). Not all formats use all effectors.

A logical page defines the usable area in lines and characters, independent of the physical printing device. For example, Format 1 uses a logical page of 60 lines by 72 characters, even though the physical paper might be 66 lines tall with 3-line margins.
sections.plainLanguage: Each format says which control codes the printer understands, and how many lines and characters fit on each page.

sections.title: Implementation and Overflow Handling
sections.content:
The RFC suggests that implementors of file-processing programs create converters between their system's local format and these standard formats. When processing a standard-format file, if the text overflows the logical page, implementations should handle the situation in one of two ways: force a form feed (new page) when too many lines are received, or discard characters that exceed the line width, then move to the next line.

The use of horizontal tabs and vertical tabs is not recommended in standard document files, since different systems handle them inconsistently, potentially defeating the goal of portability.
sections.plainLanguage: Programs reading these files should be ready to skip lines if they are too long, or to start a new page if too many lines arrive at once.
